### Review

Review is Forgejo's pull request review: approve, or request changes and say what must change; a comment neither approves nor holds anything. A pull request into `main` of `paper-repo` waits for the owners of the paths it changes, and one into its `release` or `final` waits for the approval of `internal-review-repo`, the only one counted there, of the very commit it merges: a push to it after the approval withdraws it. A review request stands until its reviewer reviews, and a review until its reviewer reviews again: nobody withdraws or dismisses another's.

### Versions and release

A version for the world's users is a merge of `main` into `release` of `paper-repo`, by a pull request that `internal-review-repo` approved and whose checks pass. The system writes the checks as commit statuses on the pull request's head (`hutian/delivery`, and the world's contract's when it holds one), and a failing one says what is missing and who provides it; nobody else writes a status. Merge with a merge commit, not a squash or a rebase, or the next version conflicts. The system publishes each version as a release of `world/result`, the world's results, with the delivery attached: the users of the world read those releases and nothing else, and every role reads them. The last approval is a merge into `final` in the same way: the system releases the world from it, at once, and nothing pushed after it is part of it. Offer a `release` version as soon as the delivery holds its main work, so that `internal-review-repo`'s review comes while there is still room to act on it; `final` is the last. Do not ask another role to review the same unchanged delivery twice merely to pass through both branches. A release goes to the world's user; no role submits it to a venue or declares a licence for it.

When the world is quiet, the system hands each remaining gap of the delivery to its owner once, and once more when `main` of `paper-repo` has moved since; if it goes quiet again before a gap, a version, an open request or a review changes, the world ends there, unless a tracked job is still running, or the world runs to a wall-clock limit with someone outside attending it and all that is left is that `paper-repo` has proposed no version, with nothing failed and nothing open but requests that `ht-human` opened and their owners have seen: then it waits instead of ending, up to that limit. So whatever needs another role's action must be open where that role owns it.

An evaluator can often afford to run a new model on only $k$ of the $N$ benchmarks a leaderboard holds. We ask which $k$ to run, how to infer the rest, and how large $k$ must be, on 238 embedding models and 328 MTEB tasks with whole organisations held out and every method scored on benchmarks that no selection rule can choose. A probabilistic factor model with a greedy design criterion beats random selection by about 1.9 points of RMSE when two or three benchmarks are run and, at a margin of a quarter of the floor, is equivalent to it from about eight. At eight benchmarks the RMSE is within 2 points of what the model's other scores give, at 32 to 50 within 1 point, and no $k$ we tried resolves neighbouring models: the floor is about 5 points, 2.5 times what the factor model predicts, and we do not find why. The closed-form risk of the model explains the design part of the error but not the floor, so it is a decomposition and not a rule for choosing $k$.
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Leaderboards hold a matrix of models by benchmarks with many holes: most models were run on a few of the benchmarks, and an evaluator with a new model can afford to run only $k$ of the $N$. Three questions follow. Which $k$ benchmarks should be run? How should the model's scores on the others be inferred from them and from the historical matrix? And how large must $k$ be before the answer is good enough? The first two are the cold-start problem of recommender systems and item selection in adaptive testing, whose machinery (a probabilistic factor model, a greedy optimal-design criterion) is classical, and we do not claim a new selection method. What is missing for benchmarks is the answer to the third question under the protocol that matches the use: whole new models, grouped by the organisation that made them, are held out, everything is fitted on the other models, and the error is measured on benchmarks that no selection rule could have chosen.

That last condition matters. If each rule is scored on the benchmarks it leaves unrun, rules that run the hardest benchmarks remove them from their own targets and can score below the error of predicting from all the other benchmarks, and the target changes with $k$. We therefore split the benchmarks at random into a pool from which a rule may choose and a target set it may not, repeat this over 50 splits, and report the excess over each model's own error when all of the pool is given, its floor (Section~\ref{sec:protocol}). Margins for what counts as a difference were set before any error was computed from the gaps between adjacent models; they proved smaller than anything attainable, so we report a second, coarser margin next to them and say which was pre-set.

On 238 embedding models and 328 tasks of the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark~\citep{muennighoff2023mteb}, with whole organisations held out, we find the following (Section~\ref{sec:experiments}).
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{How many.} The answer is a curve, not one number. Choosing the benchmarks by the factor model's design criterion, the error on the target set is within 2 points of the floor at about 8 benchmarks and within 1 point at 32 to 50; the floor itself is about 5 points, and the pre-set margin of about 0.1 point, which would resolve neighbouring models, is not reached at any $k\le109$.

\item \emph{Why the error is where it is.} A closed-form risk of the factor model, which we derive, splits the error into noise, a floor misfit, a design term and a remainder (Section~\ref{sec:theory}). I approved `paper-repo`#5 (version 1) on idea and positioning. The checks on the pull request show failure, which I didn't investigate. It still waits on `figtab-repo` and `venue-repo`.

- **Claims:** the abstract, introduction and discussion match Brief rev. 10. They claim no new method, give k as a curve in units of the floor, and report the 2.5× floor with its cause not identified. They don't claim better inference would help.
- **Citations:** every key cited in the paper exists in `refs/refs.bib`. Four entries (HELM, MMLU, MT-Bench, BigCodeBench) are unused until the transfer matrix is written.
- **One non-blocking wording fix:** the introduction says the highest-variance benchmarks "are not a substitute for the design". The experiments section shows they beat random-k by 1.3 pt at k=1, against 1.6 for the design. I asked for "do not match it beyond k=1".
- **Still to come:** the "better inference" and "second matrix" statements must be added from `experiment-repo`'s files when the P2–P6 and Open LLM Leaderboard results land, not from the Brief.
